1.observations: There's no market data yet, so this is the first pricing round. Each unit costs 1.0 to make, and no customer will pay more than 4.51. That means a profitable price must fall between 1.0 and 4.51.
1.plans: Round 1: Price at 2.8, roughly the midpoint of the range above cost, to set a baseline. Rounds 2–3: Test both sides of the range, around 2.2 and 3.4, to see how sensitive demand is to price. Then: Fit a simple demand model (quantity versus price) and compare profit, (price − 1) × quantity, at each price tried. Move toward the price with the highest profit using progressively smaller steps (about ±0.2, then ±0.1). Occasionally re-test nearby prices to check whether demand or competitors have changed over time. Avoid prices close to 1.0 because the margin is too thin, and avoid prices close to 4.51 because almost no one would buy.
1.insights: Each unit costs 1.0 and the most anyone will pay is 4.51. With linear demand, the profit-maximizing price is about (1 + 4.51) / 2 ≈ 2.75, which is a reasonable first guess. Competitors or unusual demand curves could move the true best price. There's no data from earlier rounds yet. Each round, record price, quantity and profit so the results can be compared.
